title: My Morning
blurb: 一个普通上班族的一天怎么开始
text: I get up at seven. I open the window and drink a glass of water. Then I make coffee and eat bread with eggs. My cat sits by the door and waits for food. I put on my shoes and walk to the bus stop. The bus comes at eight. I sit near the window and look at the city. Some people sleep on the bus. Some people read. I listen to music and think about my day. Work starts at nine. I like the morning. It is quiet and slow.

title: The Small Shop
blurb: 楼下那家什么都有的店
text: There is a small shop near my house. An old man and his wife run it. They open at six in the morning and close at ten at night. The shop is very small, but it has many things: water, bread, fruit, paper, soap, and even small toys. Children come after school to buy candy. The old man knows everyone's name. He always says hello. When it rains, people stand inside and talk. The shop is not just a shop. It is a warm place in our street.

title: Rainy Day
blurb: 一场雨改变了计划
text: Today it rains. I want to go to the park, but I cannot. I look out of the window. The street is wet and the sky is grey. My little sister is happy. She puts on her red boots and jumps in the water. My mother makes hot soup. We sit at the table and eat. My father tells a funny story about his first job. Everyone laughs. In the afternoon, the rain stops. The sun comes out. The air smells clean. I open the window and take a deep breath. A rainy day is not a bad day.

title: My Grandmother's Garden
blurb: 一块小小的土地，很多故事
text: My grandmother has a small garden behind her house. She grows tomatoes, beans, and flowers. Every morning she waters the plants. She talks to them, too. I think this is funny. She says, "Plants can feel you." In summer, the garden is full of green and red. We pick tomatoes and eat them with salt. They taste sweet and warm. My grandmother is old, but she works hard. She says, "If you put your hands in the earth, you never feel alone." I remember this when I am sad.

title: The Lost Dog
blurb: 一只狗、一张纸、一个邻居
text: One evening, I see a small brown dog near my building. It has no owner. It looks at me and waits. I give it some water and a piece of bread. The dog is very thin. I make a sign with the dog's photo. I write: "Do you know this dog?" I put the sign on the wall. The next morning, a woman calls me. She lives two streets away. Her father is sick and the dog ran out of the house. She cries when she sees the dog. She says thank you many times. I feel good all day.

title: The Night Market
blurb: 城市入夜后最热闹的地方
text: When the sun goes down, the night market opens. People set up their tables in the street. Someone grills meat, someone fries noodles, someone sells cold drinks. The smell is strong and the lights are bright. If you walk slowly, you can hear music, laughing, and the sound of food cooking. I usually come here with two friends. We buy small dishes and share them. The food is cheap but tastes great. The best part is not the food. It is the feeling of being outside with many people at night. The city feels different after dark. It feels more alive.

title: Learning to Ride
blurb: 一辆旧自行车和一次摔倒
text: When I was nine, my father brought home an old blue bicycle. It was too big for me. I could not touch the ground with my feet. The first day, I fell three times. My knees were red and I wanted to stop. My father said, "Today you only need to go ten meters. That is all." So I tried again. I went ten meters. The next day, twenty meters. After one week, I could ride around the whole park. I remember the wind on my face at that moment. I learned something important: big things are just many small things done one at a time.

title: A Stranger's Umbrella
blurb: 一件小事，记了很多年
text: It was raining heavily and I had no umbrella. I stood at the bus stop and waited. My clothes were wet and I was cold. A woman beside me opened her black umbrella and moved closer. She said, "Stand under it." We did not talk at first. Then she asked where I was going. She told me a little about her daughter, who was studying in another city. When my bus came, I said thank you and got on. I never saw her again and I do not know her name. But I still remember that evening. Sometimes a stranger gives you something that you carry for years.

title: The Man Who Sells Flowers
blurb: 同一个人、同一个角落、三十年
text: There is a man who sells flowers on the corner of my street. He has been there for thirty years. In winter he wears a grey coat and stands quietly in the cold. In summer he puts cold water on his flowers twice a day. Many people walk past and do not look at him. But he knows his regular customers. He knows which old lady wants white flowers, and which young man always buys one red rose on Friday. Once I asked him, "Do you get bored?" He thought for a moment and said, "A flower is never the same. Every single one opens in its own way."

title: The Sound of a City
blurb: 闭上眼睛听，城市在讲什么
text: Try closing your eyes in the middle of a city for one minute. At first you hear traffic. Then you hear smaller sounds: a key turning, a shop door opening, a child calling her mother. Someone is frying food. Someone is sweeping the street. A bus stops with a loud noise. Let us be outside with many people at night. Also there are sounds that are almost lost: a bird on a wire, water running into a drain, the soft sound of an old man's radio. A city is not just buildings. It is a thousand small noises moving at the same time. Most of us never listen.

title: Why We Forget
blurb: 遗忘不是失灵，是过滤
text:
Many people believe that a good memory means remembering everything. In fact, forgetting is part of how the brain works. Every day your brain receives thousands of pieces of information. If it kept all of them, it would be slower and less able to notice what matters. Forgetting is a filter, not a failure.

The most common cause of forgetting is not damage but absence of connection. When you learn something new, your brain creates a weak path. Each time you recall it, that path becomes stronger. If you never use it, the path slowly disappears. This is why rereading a book five times is less useful than trying to explain it to someone once.

There is also a pattern called interference. Similar information competes with itself. If you study two similar words in the same hour, you are more likely to confuse them than if you study them a day apart. Good learners do not try harder to remember. They arrange their time so that remembering is easier.

title: The Cost of Speed
blurb: 送得更快，到底谁在付钱
text:
Online shopping has changed the way we expect to live. Ten years ago, waiting a week for a package was normal. Today, many companies promise delivery in one day, or even a few hours. This speed feels like progress. But speed always has a cost, and someone has to pay it.

The first cost is paid by workers. To deliver in a few hours, warehouses must operate all night. Drivers stop when a system tells them to stop, not when they are tired. Every minute is measured by a number on a screen.

The second cost is paid by the planet. Small orders sent quickly mean more vans on the road and more packaging. A single evening delivery can use more fuel than it saves in time.

The third cost is paid by us. When everything arrives immediately, patience becomes uncomfortable. We begin to see waiting as a problem to be fixed rather than a normal part of life. Maybe the real question is not how fast we can get things, but what we are giving up to get them that fast.

title: A Language Dies
blurb: 消失的不只是词
text:
Around the world, a language disappears every two weeks. Most of these languages are spoken by small communities in remote areas, and most are not written down. When the last speaker of such a language dies, the language stops existing. But what exactly is lost?

It is easy to say that a language is just a tool, and if everyone speaks the majority language, communication becomes simpler. There is some truth in this. Speaking the same language opens schools, jobs and markets. Many parents in small communities deliberately choose not to teach their children their own language, because they want them to have an easier life.

However, a language is also a record of how a group of people solved problems. It contains knowledge of weather, plants, ocean currents, and names for relationships and feelings that other languages do not distinguish. In some languages there is a word for the smell of earth just after rain, and another for the light you see before sunrise. Losing a language is not only a loss of words. It is a loss of ways of paying attention.

title: The Quiet Trainer
blurb: 关于刻意练习的真相
text:
We often say that practice makes perfect, but not all practice is equal. In many studies of skilled people, researchers found that a person can spend twenty years doing a job and still be no better than someone with two years of experience. The difference is usually not time. It is attention.

What researchers call deliberate practice has three parts. First, it focuses on a specific weakness rather than the whole skill. A pianist does not play the entire piece again; she plays the four bars that she cannot play well. Second, it is uncomfortable. If practice feels easy, the brain is not making new connections. Third, it requires feedback, ideally from someone who can see what you cannot.

This is uncomfortable for a simple reason. Doing what we are already good at feels pleasant, and doing what we are bad at feels discouraging. Most of us avoid the second one without noticing. That is why we practice a lot and improve slowly. The real question is not how much time you spend. It is what exactly you were doing in the worst hour of it.

title: Living With Less
blurb: 把不需要的东西清出去之后
text:
Two years ago, a friend decided to remove half of everything she owned. She started with her closet, then moved to the kitchen, then the books, then the boxes in the storage room. It took her a month. Afterward, she said the strangest thing about it was not the empty space. It was how much time she had been spending on things she did not actually enjoy.

We rarely notice how much attention our possessions demand. Every object in a room asks a small question: am I clean, am I where I should be, do I still fit? Ten objects ask ten questions. A hundred objects create a constant background noise that we get used to.

Of course, having little is not automatically better than having much. Some things are worth keeping, and minimalism can become another form of hidden worry about appearance. But the experiment is useful. Once the noise is gone, you can hear which things you actually wanted, which is a question that is hard to answer while you are still surrounded by them.

title: The Attention Economy
blurb: 当你的时间成了别人的收入
text:
The phrase attention economy describes a simple idea: since information is now abundant, the scarce resource is no longer content but human attention. Companies that do not charge users must earn money in some other way, and the most common way is to sell a share of the user's time and mental activity to advertisers. This is not a hidden trick. It is the openly stated business model of most of the largest media platforms in the world.

The consequences are worth thinking about honestly. When revenue depends on how long people stay, the design process will favour whatever holds them there, regardless of whether it serves them. Features are optimised for engagement first and usefulness second. Infinite scrolling, autoplay, unpredictable notifications, countdown timers and streaks are not accidents. Each is a small engineering decision that makes leaving slightly harder than staying.

It would be too simple to say this only harms users. These platforms do connect people, help small businesses find customers, and give voice to groups who had none. The problem is not the technology but the direction in which it is optimised. A system that is rewarded for holding attention will eventually be optimised against the person whose attention it holds. Knowing this does not solve it, but it does change what you can reasonably expect from your own sense of willpower.

title: Sleep and Memory
blurb: 睡着了以后，大脑在做什么
text:
It is tempting to treat sleep as a pause in which nothing happens. Activity in the brain tells a different story. During deep sleep, the brain replays patterns of activity recorded during the day, often at much higher speed, and strengthens the connections associated with them. The information is effectively moved from temporary storage to longer-term storage. This process continues through several sleep cycles, and it is not fully replaceable with daytime rest.

What most people underestimate is how specific the effect is. In laboratory tests, participants who learn a task and then sleep perform noticeably better on it than those who stay awake the same number of hours, even though neither group practises again. The improvement is not a general sense of being refreshed. It is concentrated on the skill that was practised, which suggests that sleep is doing targeted work rather than simply resting.

There is also a less obvious cost of sleeping badly: emotional regulation deteriorates before memory does. Sleep-deprived people report more irritability and interpret neutral expressions as hostile far more often. So the next time you decide to trade two hours of sleep for two more hours of studying, the exchange may be worse than it looks. You are likely paying with the very ability you are trying to improve.

title: The Myth of the Great Idea
blurb: 创新不是灵光一闪
text:
Stories about invention tend to have the same structure. A person is struck by a sudden idea, usually in an unlikely place, and within a short time the world is different. These stories are appealing because they are simple, and they are misleading for the same reason.

If you examine the history of almost any major innovation, you find the same pattern underneath. Several people were working on similar problems at the same time, using methods that had recently become possible. The person we remember is often the one who persisted longest or understood the value first, not the one who thought of it first. The telephone, the light bulb and the theory of evolution all have contested credit, and the disputes are not a coincidence.

What this suggests is that the useful unit of creativity is not the idea but the accumulated preparation. A person who has spent years on a problem notices what others walk past, because their attention is already organised. The idea feels sudden from the inside, but from the outside it is the last step of a long process.

For anyone trying to do original work, this is good news. You cannot schedule a moment of inspiration, but you can choose to keep looking at the same problem after it stops being interesting. That appears to be the part that can be practised, and it happens to be the part most people give up on.

title: Cities for People
blurb: 一条街为什么让人想停
text:
For most of the twentieth century, city planners designed streets primarily around vehicles. Roads were widened, corners were rounded so that cars could turn quickly, and signs warned pedestrians to stay in designated places. The result was efficient for traffic and remarkably unpleasant for people, though it took decades to notice.

More recent studies of street life have produced a simple finding: what makes a street feel alive is not the number of people passing through but the number and variety of reasons to stop. A bench in the shade, a shop that opens onto the street, a tree, a place to buy something small. Where such opportunities exist, people linger, and where people linger, other people want to come. Cities that have reduced car space and given it to seating, planting and small businesses have often found that nearby shops earn more, not less.

The change is not only economic. Walking in a city where drivers expect to share the road is measurably more relaxed than walking where pedestrians are treated as an obstacle. The difference is not in the individual driver's character. It is in the design of the situation, which decides how likely it is that people will behave well toward each other. This is an uncomfortable idea for those who prefer to explain behaviour in terms of personal responsibility, and a useful one for anyone who designs anything.

title: The Limits of Measurement
blurb: 当指标变成了目标
text:
There is a persistent assumption in modern institutions that anything important can be measured, and that what is measured will improve. The assumption is not unreasonable: measurement makes comparison possible and exposes claims that would otherwise go untested. Yet the history of measurement is also a history of unintended consequences, and these are not accidents that better metrics would eliminate. They follow from a structural feature of the process itself.

When a proxy is adopted for something that cannot be observed directly, the two are almost never perfectly correlated. Once the proxy carries weight, people have an interest in moving the proxy rather than the thing it stands for. Hospitals that are judged by waiting times shorten the recorded waiting time. Schools measured by test scores narrow their teaching. In each case the measure continues to be reported accurately, which is precisely what makes the distortion difficult to detect from inside the system.

This suggests a limit that no metric can overcome. A number is a compression, and compression discards information by design. What it discards is exactly what was not anticipated when it was designed. The sensible response is therefore not to abandon measurement but to treat every indicator as a hypothesis about what matters, one that must be periodically questioned by people who are close enough to the work to notice what the number has stopped describing.

title: On Being Understood
blurb: 沟通里最难的部分
text:
The most common source of misunderstanding is not dishonesty but the assumption that words carry meaning independently of the person receiving them. In practice, every sentence arrives inside a framework of expectations, prior experience and current mood, and the listener reconstructs meaning from that framework rather than from the words alone. Two people can therefore agree on every word they exchange and still walk away with entirely different understandings of what happened.

This becomes particularly visible across distances of power or background. Someone with more authority usually believes they have been clear, because they know what they intended and their position discourages correction. Someone with less authority usually believes they have been ignored, because their interpretation never surfaced. Neither is lying. The asymmetry is in who has the opportunity to find out that they were wrong.

Repairing this cannot be achieved by insisting on greater clarity, which is what people generally mean when they ask others to communicate better. Clarity is a property of the speaker's intention. What is actually required is the more demanding habit of checking what the other person now believes, especially in the cases where you are most confident that no check is needed.

title: The Shape of Progress
blurb: 为什么感觉世界在变好又在变坏
text:
Public opinion surveys consistently reveal an odd combination: most people believe the world is becoming worse, while most objective indicators of welfare have improved substantially over the same period. This is usually explained as a failure of information, but a more interesting account concerns the different temporal shapes of good and bad news.

Improvements are gradual and distributed. Life expectancy, literacy and access to electricity rise by small annual increments that no one experiences as an event. Failures, by contrast, are sudden, concentrated and visually dramatic. Media systems, for understandable reasons of attention, report the second category almost exclusively. The result is a systematically skewed picture, not because anyone is lying, but because the exceptional is inherently more reportable than the ordinary.

There is a deeper difficulty. Progress tends to convert one set of problems into another, usually less visible, set. An increase in longevity produces new questions about care in old age. A rise in income produces new anxieties about status. Each improvement solves what was measurable and leaves behind costs that were not part of the original problem, and those costs are often experienced as decline.

Understanding this does not require optimism about the future. It requires only that we distinguish between the rate at which problems are solved and the rate at which they become visible, since the two are rarely the same.
